Good morning, Chair Cabán and Members of the Committee. I'm Cassandra Stuart, Lead Budget and Policy Analyst on Health at the New York City Independent Budget Office, IBO. I'm joined today by my colleague Ed Dolan, who is a Senior Policy Advisor at IBO. I appreciate the opportunity to discuss some of the findings of IBO's January 29th report on the Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance and Response Division, B-HEARD, with you today. The report focused on B-HEARD operations and identified several factors that should be considered for optimal performance, both for the current program size and if the program expands. A companion report focused on precinct-level data. IBO's report explores B-HEARD as it has been structured until now, a program jointly

funded, operated, and staffed by the Fire Department, FDNY, and Health and Hospitals, H and H. IBO conducted its analysis using FDNY data from the beginning of the program in June 2021 through the end of March 2025. Key takeaways from the report include, as far as eligibility, the number of calls deemed eligible for a B-HEARD response increased nine-fold between the first full quarter during which the program was operational and quarter three of Fiscal Year 2025, which is the last period that IBO has data for. While a greater share of calls has been deemed eligible for a B-HEARD response, consistently more than 40 percent since the third quarter of 2023, a declining share of eligible calls have been assigned a B-HEARD unit, down from nearly 80 percent at the beginning of the study period to 37 percent by the end. In terms of response time and time spent on scene, IBO's analysis reveals that the response times are slowing, not just for calls eligible for and receiving a B-HEARD response, but for mental health calls citywide as well. At the beginning of the study period, the median response time for B-HEARD units was 12 minutes, while at the end of the

period this had grown to 21 minutes. In the most recent period of data, the third quarter of 2025, the median response time for non-B-HEARD units was approximately 19 minutes, which is slightly faster than it was for B-HEARD units. B-HEARD teams typically spend a longer time on site than other teams responding to mental health calls, which indicates that they're taking a longer time to evaluate and resolve the cases once contact is made. In the most recent data on hand, the median time spent on scene for calls receiving a non-B-HEARD response was 19 minutes. For calls receiving a B-HEARD response, the median time spent on scene was 33 minutes. With regard to staffing, as the area covered by the program has expanded, the number of teams has also grown, though not at the same scale. B-HEARD began operation in 2021 with two teams per shift, expanding to three teams by the end of 2022, and then six by the end of 2023. By the end of 2024, with 31 precincts covered by the program, there were nine teams operating during each shift. This was also true in 2025.

As the Mamdani Administration moves toward developing its Department of Community Safety, this research provides unique insight into mental health calls, B-HEARD teams, the timing of B-HEARD responses, and geography served. Additionally, as there have been calls by Council Members and advocates to expand the program citywide and to extend hours of operation 24 hours a day, the CBO's report identifies operational challenges for consideration. B-HEARD is still considered a pilot, though it's been operating for more than four years and currently serves approximately 40 percent of the New York City population. As the program has expanded, response times have slowed. This may be in part attributable to the program's expansions outpacing the scaling of staff. Looking ahead, if the City chooses to proceed with the current program model, officials might consider what staffing levels are optimal in order to meet current demand levels in terms of the volume of mental health calls received. If the City moves forward with the Adams Administration's proposal to shift B-HEARD to H and H's sole control, factors such as call routing

without FDNY involvement, replacement of FDNY staffing, and contracting for emergency vehicles are all issues that will pose operational challenges if not addressed. Hello. Hi, Chair Cabán. Thank you for hosting today's hearing. Hi, everyone else. My name's Benjamin Heller, and I'm a Program Manager at the Vera Institute of Justice. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

Our City increasingly relies on the criminal legal system to respond to behavioral health needs, and this has contributed to the ballooning jail population, hindering the City's commitment to close Rikers Island by 2027. As of last Fiscal Year, roughly one in five people on Rikers Island had a serious mental health diagnosis. Police, courts, and jails do not provide effective treatment and incarceration often worsens mental health outcomes for individuals and for communities. To improve community-based mental health treatment, the City must start with three focus areas. First, and you've heard this a lot already, assess and scale existing services. The numbers we have are from March 2025, where the IMT waitlist was 672 people, and the ACT waitlist was 682 people. City Council must pass legislation requiring DOHMH to regularly report on these waitlists, which will enable City government to make data-driven funding decisions. Expanding capacity will allow more people to access voluntary care, improving stability without resorting to involuntary hospitalization, arrest, or incarceration.

Second, send trained peer specialists and clinicians to mental health crises, not police. Again, you've heard about this today. B-HEARD's call triage limitations and narrow eligibility criteria have meant that in the third quarter of 2025, only 41 percent of "emotionally disturbed person," or EDP, calls were deemed eligible for a B-HEARD response. To close this gap, the City should update 9-1-1 triage and dispatch to make more EDP calls, including, importantly, instances of self-harm eligible for B-HEARD. Police should not be dispatched before EMS has the chance to triage a call. Strengthening training and support for call takers will help them better determine safety risk, and embedding behavioral health professionals in dispatch centers will further improve decision-making. In addition, the City should add peer specialists to teams where appropriate, consistent with research demonstrating their effectiveness both in New York and across the country. And third, grow the behavioral health workforce. The City should mobilize a comprehensive behavioral workforce development strategy, leveraging existing assets like Health and Hospitals Peer

Academy, Community Access' Howie the Harp, and other initiatives run by OCMH. This will enable the City to scale up mental health services to meet increasing need. And without it, even with adequate funding, services won't scale. Voluntary community-based mental health services make our communities safer. By expanding and strengthening these services, the City can support people before a crisis pushes them into the criminal legal system. Incarceration cannot meet people's mental health needs, let alone do so with dignity or compassion. Thank you. CHAIRPERSON CABÁN: Thank you.

15th year as a public defender.
